title: Speech World Model: Causal State–Action Planning with Explicit Reasoning for Speech
claim: Existing models give shallow, surface-level readings of speech; ours gives deeper reasoning about intent, emotion and context.
layout: Single column of model rows, top-to-bottom, with colored highlights in the output text boxes
description: A single audio clip and an instruction ("Please analyze this speech and provide a step-by-step breakdown of your reasoning") feed in at the top through two black arrows. Below them are four rows. Each row has a model logo on the left, a green rounded box naming the model (Qwen2-Audio, Voxtral, ChatGPT, and "Speech World Model" labeled "Ours"), and a black-bordered text box with that model's response. The baseline responses are short and mostly transcribe the words or guess at a vague context. The bottom response is much longer and uses colored words (blue, red, orange, purple) to mark inferred context, tone, intent and need. The eye goes first to the audio and instruction icons, then down to the long, color-highlighted "Ours" box.
caption: Speech World Model. Demo audio link: http://bit.ly/4pBJuWP.
abstract: Current speech-language models (SLMs) typically use a cascade of speech encoder and large language model, treating speech understanding as a single black box. They analyze the content of speech well but reason weakly about other aspects, especially under sparse supervision. Thus, we argue for explicit reasoning over speech states and actions with modular and transparent decisions. Inspired by cognitive science we adopt a modular perspective and a world model view in which the system learns forward dynamics over latent states. We factorize speech understanding into four modules that communicate through a causal graph, establishing a cognitive state search space. Guided by posterior traces from this space, an instruction-tuned language model produces a concise causal analysis and a user-facing response, enabling counterfactual interventions and interpretability under partial supervision. We present a graph-based modular speech model for explicit reasoning, highlighting a path toward more transparent and controllable speech understanding.
